result.authorString: Singh P, Pancholy J, Pancholy A.

authorAffiliation.affiliation: Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Sciences, University of Texas Houston, Houston, Texas, USA.

result.abstractText:
Purpose of review

Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) is a prevalent yet underrecognized condition in postmenopausal women, characterized by progressive vulvovaginal and lower urinary tract symptoms from estrogen deficiency. Vaginal estrogen therapy is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for GSM. However, as new evidence emerges, understanding of its efficacy, safety, and use in special populations continues to evolve. This review summarizes current evidence on vaginal estrogen formulations, clinical effectiveness, safety, and therapeutic applications.

Recent findings

Recent randomized controlled trials confirm that low-dose vaginal estrogen significantly improves GSM symptoms - including vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and irritation - while restoring epithelial integrity and normalizing pH. Evidence also supports its role in reducing recurrent urinary tract infections by restoring lactobacilli-dominant flora, reinforced by a 2025 multisociety clinical guideline recommending topical, but not systemic, estrogen for this indication. Comparative studies show similar efficacy across creams, tablets, inserts, and rings, differing primarily in convenience and absorption rather than effectiveness. Large cohort studies indicate no increased risk of cardiovascular disease, venous thromboembolism, or malignancy. Use in breast cancer survivors remains controversial, but emerging data suggest minimal systemic absorption and no clear increase in recurrence risk, supporting shared decision-making. In addition, long-term outcomes show that adjunctive vaginal estrogen does not improve anatomic surgical success after native tissue apical prolapse repair. Nonhormonal therapies and agents like ospemifene or prasterone offer alternative options, though they demonstrate lower or more variable efficacy than vaginal estrogen.

Summary

Vaginal estrogen therapy is the most effective, evidence-based treatment for GSM and helps prevent recurrent urinary tract infections in postmenopausal women. Its favorable safety profile and multiple formulations enable individualized care. Recent evidence clarifies that while overall safety is reassuring, caution is necessary for breast cancer survivors using aromatase inhibitors. Additionally, longer-term perioperative trial data temper expectations regarding surgical-recurrence benefits, while confirming its value for local tissue optimization. Ongoing research should focus on long-term safety in high-risk groups and the effectiveness of emerging non-estrogen alternatives.

result.abstractText:
Background

Climacteric symptoms affect a large and growing proportion of women worldwide. Furthermore, women are increasingly participating in the workforce. Many women do not use treatment for their symptoms; however, little is known about how untreated women experience climacteric symptoms. This study examined the occurrence and severity of climacteric symptoms among full-time working women before treatment and compared their experiences across two different work environments.

Methods

A cross-sectional study was conducted in a group of Finnish women aged 52-66 years who had never used any treatment for their climacteric symptoms and were employed full-time. The data were obtained from two population-based postal surveys. Statistical techniques were used to analyse the data.

Results

The most common symptoms among all participants (n = 338) were hot flushes (80%), sweats (72%), and sleeping problems (72%). The most severe symptoms were hot flushes, sweats, and loss of sexual desire; 12% of participants experienced each of these as severe. Regarding symptom categories, vasomotor symptoms and loss of sexual desire were the most common and the most severe. Participants in either low-strain or high-strain jobs (n = 164) most often experienced five (15%) or 10 (13%) different symptoms out of 12 presented in the study questionnaire. Participants in high-strain jobs (n = 79) experienced a higher number of symptoms (p = 0.019) and more often urinary incontinence (p = 0.008) and depressive symptoms (p = 0.043) than those in low-strain jobs (n = 85). Furthermore, they experienced more severe sweats (p = 0.038).

Conclusions

Hot flushes, sweats, sleeping problems, and loss of sexual desire were both common and severe among full-time working untreated women. In addition, symptoms were more troublesome among women in high-strain than low-strain jobs. Therefore, healthcare professionals should pay special attention to the above symptoms and to women in high-strain jobs.

result.abstractText:
Objectives

This pilot study aimed to: (1) evaluate the effects of high-intensity focused electromagnetic (HIFEM) therapy on pelvic organ prolapse (POP) symptoms and pelvic floor function; (2) compare outcomes across HIFEM, pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) with biofeedback and/or electrostimulation, and usual care; and (3) explore participant acceptability of the interventions.

Materials and methods

A mixed-methods pilot study was conducted in women aged >20 years with stage I-III POP. Participants were randomized to HIFEM, PFMT, or usual care. The HIFEM group underwent twice-weekly 28-min sessions for eight weeks using a non-invasive electromagnetic chair. PFMT consisted of supervised sessions incorporating biofeedback and/or electrostimulation. Usual care included lifestyle advice. Outcomes were assessed using validated questionnaires for POP symptoms and pelvic floor distress, digital palpation, and transperineal ultrasound.

Results

Twenty-eight women completed the study (HIFEM, n = 10; PFMT, n = 9; usual care, n = 9). Compared with usual care, HIFEM significantly improved pelvic floor muscle endurance (p = 0.001), whereas PFMT significantly improved muscle strength (p = 0.034), endurance (p = 0.023), and rapid contractions (p = 0.019). Only HIFEM demonstrated significant improvements in POP symptom severity (p = 0.015) and pelvic floor distress (p = 0.041). No serious adverse events were reported. Participant satisfaction was highest in the HIFEM group (100%). Qualitative analysis supported intervention acceptability, with participants reporting increased pelvic floor awareness, improved symptom control, and enhanced psychological well-being.

Conclusions

Both HIFEM and PFMT with biofeedback appear to be safe, acceptable, and effective non-surgical treatment options for women with POP. Although no significant differences were observed between the two interventions, these findings should be interpreted with caution because of the small sample size. Larger studies are needed to confirm comparative efficacy and inform clinical implementation.

result.abstractText:
Introduction

Pelvic organ prolapse can cause urinary tract obstruction, leading to hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis, and in rare cases, renal abscess.

Case presentation

We report two elderly women with advanced pelvic organ prolapse who developed renal abscesses. Both presented with pyelonephritis and acute renal impairment accompanied by bilateral hydronephrosis. Imaging demonstrated poorly enhanced renal lesions consistent with renal abscess. Infection was successfully controlled with antimicrobial therapy, followed by surgical correction. Renal function improved, and no recurrence was observed during follow-up.

Conclusion

Advanced pelvic organ prolapse can cause severe urinary tract obstruction, leading to pyelonephritis and, in rare cases, renal abscess. Early recognition of advanced pelvic organ prolapse and urinary dysfunction, prompt infection control, and timely surgical management are essential to prevent serious complications.

result.abstractText:
Objectives

Drug treatment for overactive bladder (OAB) is changing, with an increasing share of β3-adrenoceptor agonists relative to anticholinergics, but it is not known how far this change has progressed in older people, who are most vulnerable to the risks of anticholinergics. We examined the use of these drugs in Japan by age and sex, and analyzed changes in anticholinergic burden using a large database.

Methods

We analyzed outpatient prescriptions of two β3-adrenoceptor agonists and six anticholinergics from FY2017 to FY2024, using the sex- and age-stratified tables of the NDB Open Data of Japan. Dispensed tablets were converted into patient-days, and the β3-adrenoceptor agonist share was calculated. Anticholinergic burden was measured as ACB-weighted prescription volume (patient-days multiplied by the anticholinergic cognitive burden score). Because FY2021-FY2022 was a period of nationwide generic supply disruption, FY2018 and FY2024 were used as endpoints when estimating change over time.

Results

The β3-adrenoceptor agonist share rose from 36.2% to 64.9%, but anticholinergic use fell only slightly (3.10 × 108 to 2.94 × 108 tablets; -5.0%). In FY2024, the β3-adrenoceptor agonist share was higher in men than in women in every age group, and the difference widened with age (+1.2 percentage points at 50-54 years and +14.2 at ≥ 90 years). ACB-weighted prescription volume was higher in women than in men, and the female-to-male ratio rose with age (1.1 at 65-74 years, 1.6 at 75-84 years, and 2.8 at ≥ 85 years). Between FY2018 and FY2024, prescription volume fell by about 20% at 65-74 and 75-84 years, but the fall was smallest in women aged ≥ 85 years (-11.3%).

Conclusions

The β3-adrenoceptor agonist share for OAB has continued to increase in Japan, but this change appears slower in older women, in whom anticholinergic exposure remains high.

Introduction

Pelvic and genital pain is a common symptom among women with endometriosis and may negatively affect sexual functioning. Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) may improve sexual functioning, but whether this applies to women with endometriosis remains to be explored. This study is a planned secondary analysis in which we aimed to examine how general exercise and PFMT, when added to pain management, affect sexual functioning among women with endometriosis.

Material and methods

Planned secondary analysis of a two-armed, parallel-group randomized controlled trial with intention-to-treat analysis. Women aged 18-45 years with laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis and experiencing pelvic/genital pain were eligible. All participants attended a pain management course. In addition to weekly home training, the exercise group (n = 41) participated in weekly supervised general exercise training, including PFMT, for 4 months. The control group (n = 40) received no further intervention. Between-group differences in sexual function were assessed using the total score of the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) at the end of the 4-month intervention and at the 12-month follow-up. We also examined differences in the subdomains-desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain-at these time points.

Clinical trial registration

NCT05091268.

Results

Four months post-intervention, the exercise group showed significantly higher total FSFI scores compared to the control group (mean difference = 3.52, 95% CI 0.49-6.54, p = 0.023). Significant between-group differences were also observed for the subdomains lubrication (mean difference = 0.90, 95% CI 0.17-1.63, p = 0.016) and orgasm (mean difference = 0.81, 95% CI 0.07-1.55, p = 0.033). No significant between-group differences were found for desire, arousal, or pain at the end of the 4-month intervention, or at 12 months follow-up for any domain.

Conclusions

The findings suggest that the combined intervention of supervised exercise and PFMT, when added to pain management, may lead to short-term improvements in sexual function at the end of the 4-month intervention. Whether this effect is attributable to general exercise, PFMT, or their combination cannot be determined from the present study. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously due to differences in sexual activity status between groups.

result.abstractText:
Introduction

Childbirth-related perineal trauma (CRPT) is the most common complication of vaginal birth, yet its associations with mental health and other health outcomes remain poorly described. This study examined the annual incidence of recorded CRPT by tear degree and investigated its association with mental health and other health outcomes.

Material and methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study using Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum primary care data linked with Hospital Episode Statistics, including women aged ≥16 years who had given birth vaginally between 1st January 2005 and 31st December 2019. Exposure was defined as recorded CRPT of any degree including episiotomy. Annual incidence of CRPT was calculated as a percentage of all births. Cox proportional hazards regression models compared short-, medium-, and long-term (<1 year, 1-5 years, and >5 years post-childbirth) outcomes between women with and without CRPT. We conducted subgroup analyses by degree of tear and in women with spontaneous vertex births, and a sensitivity analysis restricted to first birth.

Results

Incidence of recorded CRPT increased from 43.4% to 48.8% between 2005 and 2019. Compared to women without CRPT, those with CRPT had a higher risk of anxiety (aHR 1.19, 95%CI 1.17, 1.22) or depression (aHR 1.23, 95%CI 1.21, 1.25) within 1 year postpartum, with elevated risks persisting beyond 5 years and across all degrees of tear. Women with 1st/2nd degree tears or episiotomy had a higher hazard of post-traumatic stress disorder 1-5 years postpartum. CRPT was associated with increased hazard of urinary incontinence, dyspareunia, reduced libido, vaginal discharge, general and perineal pain, and prolapse in all follow-up periods. Fecal incontinence was increased in women with episiotomy or 3rd/4th degree tears, persisting long-term for severe tears. CRPT was associated with 32% higher risk of antibiotic prescription compared to no CRPT (OR 1.32, 95%CI 1.30, 1.33) within 6 weeks postpartum.

Conclusions

Recorded CRPT was associated with increased risks of diagnosed anxiety and depression in short-, medium- and long-term post-childbirth, irrespective of tear severity, as well as higher risks of other adverse outcomes, including urinary incontinence, pain, and sexual dysfunction. Addressing CRPT should be prioritized to improve women's health and well-being.

Introduction and objectives

Overactive bladder (OAB) is highly prevalent among women. Energy-based treatments, such as radiofrequency (RF), have shown promising results in urinary incontinence, but evidence for OAB remains limited. This study evaluated the efficacy of microablative RF compared with sham in women with OAB over 6 months of follow-up.

Methods

Bicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group trial was conducted between March 2023 and July 2025 at two public hospitals in Brazil (UNICAMP and UFPR), following CONSORT guidelines. Women aged 45-65 years with OAB or mixed urinary incontinence with urgency predominance were randomized (1:1) to RF or sham treatment, both combined with behavioral therapy (BT). Participants underwent 3 monthly sessions. Assessments included validated questionnaires (ICIQ-OAB, ICIQ-OAB QoOL, ICIQ-UI SF, ICIQ-VS, FSFI), bladder diaries, pelvic floor evaluation (PERFECT and manometry), VHI, and vaginal cytology. The primary outcome was changes in ICIQ-OAB score at 6 months. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle.

Results

140 women were randomized (RF = 72; sham = 68). Both groups showed significant improvement in OAB symptoms, with effects maintained at follow-up. ICIQ-OAB QoL, ICIQ UI-SF and ICIQ-VS improved in both groups. In the RF group, pelvic floor tone normalized and pain on palpation decreased (p = 0.026 and p = 0.035), repetitions of sustained and rapid contractions improved (p = 0.039, p = 0.015), with more adverse events than sham (44.2% vs. 22.9%; p = 0.025).

Conclusion

RF combined with BT improved OAB symptoms with effects sustained at 6 months. However, no superiority over sham treatment was observed, reinforcing the value of BT as the, current first-line treatment recommendation for patients with OAB.

Background

Urinary incontinence is highly prevalent among older women, affecting more than one-third of this population and significantly impairing quality of life, independence, and healthcare utilization. Older women often present with complex needs that may require broader rehabilitation strategies.

Methods

This systematic review evaluated randomized controlled trials of physical therapy interventions for urinary incontinence in older women. PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched to October 2025. Eligible studies included women ≥60 years and assessed interventions such as Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), bladder training, Yoga, Pilates, general resistance training, electrical stimulation, or multimodal programs. Methodological quality was appraised using the PEDro scale, and random-effects meta-analysis was performed where appropriate.

Results

Twenty studies involving 2002 women across 13 countries were included. Eleven trials were rated as good quality and nine as fair. Meta-analysis demonstrated that PFMT significantly reduced urinary incontinence severity compared with usual care (SMD = -1.27, 95% CI: -2.18 to -0.36, p = 0.006). Multimodal programs combining PFMT with mobility, strength, or fall-prevention training also showed significant benefits (SMD = -0.98, 95% CI: -1.60 to -0.36, p = 0.002). Comparative studies indicated that PFMT was similarly effective to Yoga and Pilates, while adjuncts such as general resistance training or tibial nerve stimulation provided additional improvements.

Conclusion

Physical therapy interventions, particularly PFMT and multimodal programs, are effective in reducing urinary incontinence severity and improving functional outcomes among older women. These findings support prioritizing physical therapy as an important management strategy, with multimodal approaches offering added value for enhancing functional independence and fall prevention.

Background

Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is a common condition affecting elderly women. This study aimed to evaluate whether combining pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) with electromagnetic stimulation (EMS) provides better outcomes than PFMT alone, using objective three-dimensional (3D) ultrasound parameters.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective analysis of 240 elderly women with POP treated between January 2023 and January 2025. Based on the received treatment, patients were grouped to a PFMT group (n = 114) or a PFMT-EMS group (n = 126). All patients underwent a standardized 15 week intervention. We assessed pelvic floor 3D ultrasound parameters, Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) stage, pelvic floor muscle strength metrics, and symptom scores pre- and post-treatment.

Results

This analysis included 240 patients. The PFMT-EMS group showed significantly greater improvement in key ultrasound parameters, including a smaller levator ani hiatus area on Valsalva (P < 0.001) and reduced bladder neck descent (P < 0.001). This group also achieved better POP-Q stage improvement (P = 0.013), greater enhancement in muscle strength and symptom relief (all P < 0.001), and a higher total effective rate (P = 0.027).

Conclusion

Combining PFMT with EMS produces superior anatomical and functional outcomes in elderly women with POP than PFMT alone.

result.abstractText:
Objective

To summarize the available evidence on the management of cervical cancer in older women across early and advanced disease stages, with particular attention to treatment selection, feasibility, tolerance, and specific clinical situations, including cervical cancer associated with pelvic organ prolapse.

Methods

A narrative review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library. Studies addressing surgery, radiotherapy, concurrent chemoradiotherapy, brachytherapy, para-aortic lymphadenectomy, cervical cancer associated with pelvic organ prolapse, and pre-treatment geriatric assessment were considered. The evidence was synthesized qualitatively according to six predefined clinical questions.

Results

In early-stage disease, radical hysterectomy is feasible in selected fit elderly patients but is associated with increased perioperative morbidity, with advancing age. The available evidence does not establish whether surgery or definitive radiotherapy provides superior oncological outcomes in this population. In locally advanced cervical cancer, concurrent chemoradiotherapy appears to improve survival compared with radiotherapy alone in selected older patients, but with increased toxicity. Brachytherapy is associated with improved local control and survival, yet its use decreased with advancing age. No age-specific evidence demonstrated a survival benefit form pretreatment para-aortic lymphadenectomy. Data on cervical cancer associated with pelvic organ prolapse are limited to heterogeneous case reports and small retrospective studies. Pretreatment geriatric assessment influences treatment decisions in mixed cancer populations, but cervical cancer-specific outcome data are lacking.

Conclusion

Age-specific evidence remains limited and largely retrospective, and chronological age alone should not determine access to standard treatment. Treatment selection requires integration of tumor characteristics, frailty, comorbidities, functional status, expected treatment tolerance, quality of life, and patient preferences.

result.abstractText:
Objective

Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is a prevalent and costly condition, with an estimated lifetime risk of surgery reaching 20% by the age of 80 years. Single-incision mini-slings (SIMS) represent the latest advancement in midurethral sling technology, offering a minimally invasive alternative to traditional retropubic and transobturator tapes (TOT). Studies indicate comparable subjective and objective cure rates between SIMS and TOT, with potential advantages in postmenopausal women owing to earlier mobilization and reduced morbidity. The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of SIMS under local anesthesia in the management of SUI.

Methods

A prospective cohort study was conducted in a tertiary academic urogynecology unit from December 2019 to December 2024. Consecutive patients meeting the inclusion criteria were enrolled following a standardized diagnostic and treatment protocol. Informed consent was obtained, and ethical approval was granted by the institutional review board. All patients underwent SIMS placement (Altis©, Coloplast) performed by two experienced urogynecologists under local anesthesia. Sling tensioning was performed via a standardized cough stress test at bladder volumes equal to normal voiding volume, as per pre-operative urodynamics. Patients were followed for 3 weeks and 12 months post-surgery. Data analysis was conducted using Microsoft Excel. Descriptive statistics were applied, and paired t-tests compared pre- and post-operative results. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.

Results

A total of 124 women underwent SIMS for SUI, with a mean age of 63.8 ± 11.1 years and a body mass index (BMI, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters) of 29.0 ± 4.3. Among them, 21.8% had severe and 78.2% had moderate SUI, while 30.6% presented with mixed urinary incontinence (MUI). Pre-operatively, mean International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire (ICIQ) Urinary Incontinence Short Form (ICIQ-UI-SF) and Female Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (ICIQ-FLUTS) scores were 14.3 ± 2.4 and 19.0 ± 6.0, respectively. All surgeries were performed in an ambulatory setting, with 95.2% discharged the same day. The mean surgical time was 31.5 ± 8.0 min, and peri-operative pain was 2.8 ± 1.8/10. At discharge, all but one patient had a negative stress test, and 99.2% would recommend the procedure. At 12 months, the composite outcome was successful for 103 (83.1%) patients, with an objective cure rate of 94.3% and a subjective cure rate of 83.1%. A clinically important difference in ICIQ-FLUTS was observed in 92.7% of cases. Patient Global Impression of Improvement (PGI-I, scores 1 or 2) was reported by 93.5%, and Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S, score 1) was reported by 83.9%. There were no cases of bladder perforation, major bleeding, mesh erosion, or reoperation.

Conclusion

The present study evaluates SIMS under local anesthesia as a minimally invasive and effective treatment for SUI, highlighting its potential benefits in post-operative recovery and resource optimization. The findings contribute to the ongoing advancements in SUI management, particularly in addressing modern healthcare challenges.

result.abstractText:
Background

Rectal prolapse is a condition most prevalent among older women that impacts daily quality of life. Current national guidelines recommend elective multidisciplinary management for rectal prolapse care. Despite these recommendations, little is known about the frequency and predisposing factors of emergent rectal prolapse admissions or their associated outcomes.

Objective

To quantify emergent admission rates among people with rectal prolapse, compare outcomes of emergent v. elective admissions, and identify factors associated with emergent admission.

Design

Retrospective cohort analysis.

Settings

Nationwide inpatient Sample, 2017 to 20.

Patients

Adults aged 18 years and older admitted with a diagnosis of rectal prolapse.

Main outcome measures

Primary exposure was admission type (emergent vs elective). Primary outcomes included length of stay, in-hospital mortality, and discharge disposition. Secondary outcomes included performance of rectal prolapse repair and operative approach.

Results

A total of 7,555 adult patients were admitted with a diagnosis of rectal prolapse. Of these, 1,681 (22.2%) admissions were emergent. Emergent admissions were associated with longer length of stay, higher in-hospital mortality, lower likelihood of discharge home, and greater need for postacute care. Surgical intervention was less common among emergent admissions, and perineal procedures were more common. On multivariable analysis, older age, Black and Hispanic race, Medicare, Medicaid and self-pay status, homelessness, lower neighborhood income, schizophrenia, substance use disorder, eating disorder, dementia, intellectual disability, and higher comorbidity burden were independently associated with emergent admission. Female sex and depression were associated with lower odds of emergent admission.

Limitations

The database captures inpatient hospitalizations only and diagnoses and procedures are identified using administrative billing codes.

Conclusions

Emergent admissions accounted for a substantial number of rectal prolapse hospitalizations nationally and were associated with socioeconomic vulnerability, multimorbidity, psychiatric and cognitive conditions, and worse clinical outcomes. These findings highlight existing differences in healthcare utilization for this surgical patient population. See Video Abstract.

result.abstractText: Background/Objective: Urinary incontinence (UI) negatively affects wellbeing. As it is often seen as a normal part of aging, management is frequently delayed or ignored, challenging healthy aging. This study aimed to characterize UI in community-dwelling older women by assessing sociodemographic aspects, symptoms, pelvic floor muscle strength, urinary habits, and perceptions regarding UI. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study in older women from four communities in Chile. After educational sessions on UI, women voluntarily enrolled. We applied the ICIQ-SF, and pelvic floor muscle strength was evaluated using the Modified Oxford Scale. We also collected information on UI-related topics. Results: Among 32 older women assessed, 40.6% had stress UI, 3.1% had urgency UI, and 56.3% exhibited mixed UI. The mean ICIQ-SF score was 13.75 ± 3.5, corresponding to severe UI, with a mean score of interference on daily life of 6.75 ± 1.92. Older women exhibited low pelvic floor muscle strength (Oxford: 1.97 ± 1.03), a high prevalence of cystocele (84.4%; n = 27), and coexisting fecal incontinence (40.6%; n = 13). An association between UI severity and pelvic floor muscle strength was evaluated (Spearman's ρ = -0.242, n = 32), but the weak inverse correlation was not statistically significant (p = 0.180). Conclusions: Community-dwelling older women with UI exhibited substantial symptom severity accompanied by low pelvic floor muscle strength, pelvic organ prolapse, coexisting fecal incontinence, and potentially modifiable UI-related habits and perceptions. Although these findings derive from an exploratory sample, they highlight opportunities for community-based education, early detection, and pelvic floor health interventions to support healthy aging.

Background

Menopausal symptoms significantly impair women's quality of life, and conventional menopausal hormone therapy carries risks of clinical contraindications and adverse effects. Digital health interventions (DHIs) are gaining attention as a promising non-pharmacological alternative for sustained symptom management. This study aimed to comprehensively evaluate the clinical efficacy of DHIs for peri- and postmenopausal women.

Methods

We searched 6 databases for eligible clinical studies from inception to May 2025. The methodological quality of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2. For non-randomized studies, the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions and the National Institutes of Health Quality Assessment Tool were used. The certainty of evidence for outcomes reported by RCTs was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.

Results

A total of 8 studies involving 17,420 participants were included. DHIs utilized various mechanisms, including cognitive behavioral therapy, hypnotherapy, biofeedback-based pelvic floor muscle training, cognitive training, behavior change and self-care models, and personalized healthcare. Overall, DHIs were associated with improvements in vasomotor symptoms, psychological distress, pelvic floor dysfunction, and cognitive decline. However, there was high methodological heterogeneity and study design limitations; both RCTs were rated as having "some concerns" regarding risk of bias. According to the GRADE assessment, the certainty of evidence was low for Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) and very low for Midlife Women's Symptom Index (MSI).

Conclusion

DHIs demonstrate clinical potential as a non-pharmacological alternative for managing menopausal symptoms. Large-scale, well-designed RCTs with longer follow-up are needed. Trial registration/Protocol registration: PROSPERO (CRD420251042496).

Objective

This study characterizes urinary incontinence (UI) burden and symptom-based UI phenotype transitions 1 year after colpocleisis in older women with advanced pelvic organ prolapse.

Methods

This single-center retrospective cohort included women aged 60 years or older undergoing colpocleisis for advanced or recurrent pelvic organ prolapse between August 2019 and May 2025. Paired analyses included women with 1-year urinary follow-up. UI burden was assessed using the International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form (ICIQ-SF), and symptom-based phenotypes were classified as stress UI (SUI), urgency UI (UUI), or mixed UI (MUI).

Results

Of 505 women, 495 completed 1-year follow-up; 258 had preoperative UI. Any UI decreased from 52.1% to 39.8% (paired absolute risk difference -12.3 percentage points, 95% confidence interval [CI] -17.8 to -6.7; P < 0.001). The median ICIQ-SF total score declined from 4.0 (interquartile range [IQR] 0.0-7.0) to 0.0 (IQR 0.0-5.0), with a Hodges-Lehmann paired estimate of -0.5 (95% CI -1.5 to 0.0; P < 0.001). UUI and MUI decreased, whereas SUI increased modestly. Among 237 women without preoperative UI, 65 (27.4%) developed de novo UI, of which 55.4% was slight and none was very severe. Baseline UUI most often transitioned to no UI, whereas baseline MUI showed the broadest postoperative distribution.

Conclusion

Colpocleisis was associated with reduced UI burden and distinct symptom-based phenotype transitions at 1 year. Descriptive transition patterns might inform preoperative counseling but should not be interpreted as an individual prediction tool.

Importance

Prophylactic midurethral sling (MUS) placement can prevent de novo stress urinary incontinence (SUI) after pelvic organ prolapse (POP) repair, but the concern about additional MUS-related adverse events remains.

Objective

The objective of this study was to compare postoperative outcomes between women with and without preoperative SUI after undergoing concomitant POP repair and MUS placement.

Study design

This retrospective cohort study included women undergoing POP repair with concurrent MUS placement between 2017 and 2023. Patients in the prophylactic group did not have preoperative SUI, whereas those in the nonprophylactic group did. The primary outcome was postoperative SUI. Secondary outcomes included recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI), voiding difficulty, overactive bladder symptoms, pelvic pain, and mesh complications. Multivariate logistic regression was used to adjust for potential confounders.

Results

Of 1,132 women, there were 409 (36.1%) prophylactic and 723 (63.9%) nonprophylactic MUS procedures. Women in the prophylactic group were significantly older, predominantly postmenopausal, of lower body mass index, and more commonly had stage 3 POP and underwent sacrocolpopexy. Median follow-up was 12 months. Postoperative SUI occurred less frequently in the prophylactic group (1.7% vs 5.8%; P=0.001). Women with a prophylactic MUS were nearly 3 times less likely to have postoperative SUI (adjusted odds ratio, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.14-0.72). Postoperative recurrent UTIs were less common in the prophylactic group (1.5% vs 4.4%; P=0.008), whereas other adverse events were comparable between groups.

Conclusions

Women without preoperative SUI had lower rates of postoperative SUI after concomitant POP repair and MUS placement, with similar rates of adverse events.

result.abstractText: Pelvic floor dysfunction is a common condition in adult women. In addition to the levator ani, the obturator internus, a lateral pelvic wall muscle, has been suggested to be anatomically and mechanically associated with pelvic floor morphology. Here, we quantitatively characterized age-related morphological changes in the obturator internus and levator ani using geometric morphometric analysis. We hypothesized a significant association between principal components accounting for major shape variation and age. This cross-sectional study included 27 adult women aged 25-83 years with gynecological conditions but without pelvic floor disorders based on clinical assessment and imaging findings. Standardized pelvic magnetic resonance imaging scans were obtained between April 2024 and July 2024 at a single tertiary care center. Elliptic Fourier analysis was applied to the segmented obturator internus contours; a landmark-based method was used to evaluate the combined shape of the obturator internus and levator ani. Principal component analysis and linear regression were performed to assess associations with age. Procrustes analysis of variance was used to evaluate the overall shape-age relationships. Elliptic Fourier analysis revealed that increasing age was significantly associated with relative narrowing of the superior portion, an inferior morphological shift of the medial surface groove, and increased prominence of the medial eminence of the obturator internus. A landmark-based analysis revealed similar age-related shape changes, including inferiorly directed shape changes of the groove, verticalization of the levator ani, and widening of the levator hiatus. Procrustes analysis revealed a significant relationship between age and overall shape variation. Aging was associated with coordinated age-related morphological remodeling of the obturator internus and levator ani.

Introduction and hypothesis

Urinary incontinence (UI) is common after childbirth, but uptake of care may be limited. We aimed to describe UI burden, pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), care-seeking, and support preferences among parous women in Japan.

Methods

In March 2026, 1000 parous women aged 20-49 years completed a cross-sectional online survey with equal age-decade quotas. This unweighted, non-probability sample was not nationally representative. Current UI was operationalized as an International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Urinary Incontinence Short Form (ICIQ-UI SF) total score ≥ 1. Modified Poisson regression estimated adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs).

Results

Overall, 55.8% met this inclusive criterion (558/1000; 95% confidence interval [CI] 52.7-58.9), while 28.1% had moderate-to-severe UI (281/1000; 95% CI 25.4-31.0). Only 1.7% reported a hospital visit specifically for UI; among 416 women reporting leakage on the ICIQ-UI SF frequency item, 56.2% had no intention of seeking care. Overall, 20.7% reported performing PFMT after the most recent delivery and 16.3% reported receiving PFMT instruction. Among women perceiving PFMT as important (51.6%), those who did not report performing it (35.8% overall) less often reported receiving instruction than those who did (6.4% vs 58.9%). Self-reported UI during pregnancy showed the strongest association with current UI (aPR 1.85, 95% CI 1.66-2.07). PFMT instruction was the most frequently selected support option (45.0%).

Conclusions

In this unweighted, non-probability Japanese online-panel sample, UI symptoms coexisted with limited healthcare contact; only a minority reported performing PFMT. The findings support prospective evaluation of accessible PFMT assessment and instruction but not population-level or causal inference.

result.abstractText: Background/Objectives: This study examined whether adding relaxation-oriented immersive virtual reality (VR) to pelvic floor muscle electrostimulation with electromyographic (EMG) biofeedback was associated with additional improvement in incontinence-related quality of life among postmenopausal women. Methods: In this exploratory non-randomized controlled pilot trial, 40 postmenopausal women received electrostimulation with EMG biofeedback alone (ES; n = 20) or the same intervention preceded by VR (VR + ES; n = 20). Participants completed eight sessions over 2 weeks and were assessed at baseline (T0), post-intervention (T1), and 2-week follow-up (T2); T1 was the prespecified primary assessment. The primary outcome was the Incontinence Quality of Life Questionnaire (I-QOL) total score. Secondary outcomes included pelvic floor EMG, bladder-diary variables, other quality-of-life measures, perceived stress, and self-esteem. Baseline-adjusted linear mixed models were used. The registry record was submitted before enrollment (NCT07070063). Results: Thirty-six participants contributed to the primary analysis. The adjusted between-group difference in I-QOL was -1.65 points at T1 (95% CI, -10.03 to 6.74; p = 0.70) and -4.00 points at T2 (95% CI, -12.38 to 4.39; p = 0.35). Adjusted contrasts were non-significant for the remaining questionnaire and EMG outcomes. Selected bladder-diary outcomes differed between groups, but these analyses were exploratory, unadjusted for multiple comparisons, and did not directly quantify urinary leakage. Conclusions: The study did not detect a statistically significant additional improvement in incontinence-related quality of life with adjunctive VR. Confidence intervals remained compatible with potentially meaningful effects in either direction. Given the small sample and non-randomized design, the findings are preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

Importance

Chronic anticoagulation has been identified as a risk factor for postoperative complications in other specialties, but there is a paucity of data on its effect on older women undergoing obliterative prolapse repair.

Objective

The objective of this study was to assess whether chronic anticoagulation is associated with increased serious adverse events (SAEs) after obliterative prolapse surgery.

Study design

This was a retrospective cohort analysis of women 65 years or older undergoing obliterative prolapse repair at 2 academic institutions from 2016 to 2023. Patients were identified by Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code and grouped by preoperative chronic anticoagulation status. The composite primary outcome was defined as SAE within 8 weeks of surgery. Multivariable logistic regression was performed, controlling for relevant variables with P <0.10 on univariate analysis.

Results

Among the 777 older women who underwent obliterative surgery, 97 (12.5%) were chronically anticoagulated. The most commonly used anticoagulants were apixaban (n = 37, 38.1%) and clopidogrel (n = 31, 32%), with 21.7% reporting concomitant use of aspirin. Anticoagulated individuals were more likely to be current smokers and to have a history of venous thromboembolism, myocardial infarction, and stroke (P < 0.05). Chronically anticoagulated women had 1.72 times greater adjusted odds of experiencing SAE (95% CI, 1.02-2.91). Chronic anticoagulation was associated with an increased incidence of readmission, cardiac complications, transfusion, hematoma, and organ-space surgical site infection (P < 0.05). Rates of SAEs were highest in individuals taking rivaroxaban (35.7%) and those taking concomitant aspirin (38.1%).

Conclusions

Chronic anticoagulation is associated with increased odds of SAE in older women undergoing obliterative prolapse surgery. Physicians should consider this additional risk in surgical decision making and counseling on anticoagulant suspension and resumption perioperatively.

result.abstractText: Urinary incontinence (UI), defined as the involuntary leakage of urine, is a common condition that affects women's quality of life and overall health. UI becomes more frequent with age and is also observed during pregnancy and postpartum. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine the prevalence of UI among women. A literature search was conducted between December 2024 and February 2025 in Google Scholar, PubMed, Web of Science, Türkiye Citation Index, Ulakbim, and Turkish Medline. Risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Forty-five studies published between 2005 and 2025, including 41,038 participants, were analyzed. The pooled prevalence of UI among women aged 15 years and older was 36.7%. Prevalence estimates for stress, urgency, and mixed UI were 31.1%, 18.4%, and 27.5%. Definitions used influenced prevalence rates. Planning and delivering appropriate health services based on these findings can contribute to protecting and improving women's health. In Türkiye, it would be beneficial to develop a policy to raise awareness about urinary incontinence in women and to evaluate the condition. Interventions can be implemented nationwide in this way.

Purpose

This study aimed to examine the associations among sarcopenia, lower urinary tract symptoms, and anxiety in urinary incontinence in community-dwelling older women.

Methods

We analyzed data from 194 older women (mean age: 74.7 ± 5.8 years) who participated in a community cohort study. Sarcopenia was defined according to the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia 2019 criteria. Lower urinary tract symptoms were classified into two groups based on the presence or absence of urinary incontinence, increased daytime frequency, and nocturia. Anxiety was classified into two groups based on the presence or absence of urinary incontinence-related anxiety in urinary incontinence. Associations among sarcopenia, lower urinary tract symptoms, and anxiety in urinary incontinence were examined using binary logistic regression analysis.

Results

Of the participants, 31 (16%) were classified as having sarcopenia, of whom 67.7% had nocturia, which was a significantly higher proportion (42.9%) than that in those without sarcopenia (p = 0.011). Multivariate analysis revealed that sarcopenia was significantly associated with nocturia (odds ratio: 2.61; 95% confidence interval: 1.05-6.49). No association was observed between sarcopenia and urinary incontinence, increased daytime frequency, or anxiety in urinary incontinence.

Conclusions

Sarcopenia was independently associated with nocturia in community-dwelling older women, regardless of the presence or absence of concomitant lower urinary tract symptoms. These findings suggest that sarcopenia is related to nocturia and highlight the potential importance of evaluating sarcopenia in addition to pelvic floor muscles in older women.

Objective

The purpose of this study was to observe the relationship between sarcopenic obesity (SO) and urinary incontinence (UI) among adult women in the United States.

Methods

A retrospective study was conducted on United States adult women aged over 20 years. Data were extracted from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2001-2006, and 2011-2018 cycles. UI diagnosis was collected via self-report questionnaire about kidney conditions. Sarcopenic obesity was defined as appendicular skeletal muscle mass divided by weight less than 23.47 % and percentage of fat mass equal to or greater than 40 %.

Results

The prevalence rates of stress UI, urgency UI, and mixed UI were 39.6 %, 24.4 %, and 15.7 %, respectively. In univariate logistic regression, women with sarcopenic obesity had higher odds of stress UI, urgency UI, and mixed UI compared to the normal group (odds ratio = 2.048, 2.219, and 2.532, P < 0.001). After adjusting for confounders, the odds remained significantly elevated (adjusted odds ratio = 1.485, 1.554, and 1.663, P < 0.001).

Conclusion

The present study demonstrates that sarcopenic obesity was closely associated with an increased odds of UI in United States adult women.

result.abstractText:
Background

Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) affects nearly half of U.S. women. Central adiposity, measured by waist circumference, may be more pathophysiologically relevant than BMI due to its direct impact on intra-abdominal pressure. However, whether age modifies this association remains unclear.

Methods

We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 894 non-pregnant women (55.8 % with SUI) from the 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). Weighted multivariable logistic regression examined associations between SUI and waist circumference, age, parity, race/ethnicity, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). An age × waist circumference interaction term was tested, followed by age-stratified analyses using 41 years as the cutoff.

Results

Parity ((odds ratio (OR) = 1.17, 95 % CI: 1.01-1.36; p = 0.027), race (non-Hispanic White vs. other: OR = 1.13, p = 0.030; non-Hispanic Black vs. other: OR = 0.78, p = 0.001), and COPD (OR = 1.28, p = 0.007) were independently associated with SUI. The age-waist circumference interaction was significant (p = 0.020). In women < 41 years (n = 365), only parity and race predicted SUI. In women ≥ 41 years (n = 529), each 1-cm increase in waist circumference increased SUI odds by 0.3 % (OR = 1.003, 95 % CI: 1.001-1.006; p = 0.013), equivalent to a 1.5 % increase per 5-cm increment, independent of COPD and race.

Conclusions

Age fundamentally modifies the SUI-adiposity relationship, rendering central obesity a key modifiable risk factor exclusively in women ≥ 41 years while parity dominates in younger women. These findings advocate for age-specific prevention strategies prioritizing waist circumference reduction in older women and pelvic floor rehabilitation post-childbirth in younger women.

Importance

Limited data describe short-term Medicare-allowed amounts associated with treatments for stress urinary incontinence (SUI).

Objective

The objective of this study was to compare total Medicare-allowed amounts for pelvic floor muscle therapy (PFMT), pessary, and sling surgery as the first SUI treatments observed.

Study design

We analyzed 5% Medicare fee-for-service claims from 2008 through 2016 for women aged 66 years or older with SUI or mixed urinary incontinence. Episode allowed amounts were summed for 90 days after PFMT or pessary treatment and 180 days after sling surgery, adjusted to 2016 dollars, and modeled using log-linear regression.

Results

Among 16,695 beneficiaries (median age: 76 y; 92.9% White), 46.2% received pessary, 33.3% PFMT, and 20.5% sling surgery. From 2008 to 2016, PFMT increased from 24.8% to 43.5% of observed treatments, whereas sling surgery decreased from 27.9% to 9.8% (P<0.01 for both). Median total allowed amounts were $654 (IQR, $327-$1,340) for PFMT over 90 days, $766 (IQR, $458-$1,244) for pessary over 90 days, and $3,663 (IQR, $1,511-$4,173) for sling over 180 days. Facility-related amounts represented 73% of aggregate sling allowed amounts. Compared with pessary, sling was associated with a 3.3-fold higher allowed amount. Clinician specialty, urinary tract infection, geographic region, and Medicare-only coverage were independently associated with allowed amounts.

Conclusions

Short-term Medicare-allowed amounts varied by treatment, specialty, and region. Because observation windows differed and the data are historical, these estimates are treatment-specific benchmarks rather than current head-to-head comparisons.

Introduction and hypothesis

Pelvic organ prolapse is a common condition in older women requiring surgical correction. The benefits of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) have been demonstrated in gynecological procedures, but there are still few data on its use in older patients (aged 60 years and above) undergoing transvaginal pelvic floor reconstruction. This study evaluates the effectiveness and safety of ERAS compared with conventional perioperative care, specifically in this older population.

Methods

A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases were searched for randomized and observational studies comparing ERAS with conventional care in older patients undergoing transvaginal pelvic floor reconstruction. Outcomes assessed were time to first intestinal exhaust, ambulation, urinary catheterization duration, hospital stay, operative time, bleeding volume, 30-day readmission, and reoperation rates. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently, and pooled analyses were conducted using a random-effects model.

Results

Nine studies involving 1,585 patients were included. ERAS significantly reduced time to first intestinal exhaust, ambulation, urinary catheter removal, and postoperative length of stay compared with conventional care. No significant differences were observed in operative duration, intraoperative bleeding, 30-day readmission, or reoperation rates.

Conclusions

For older patients undergoing transvaginal pelvic floor reconstruction, ERAS enhances postoperative recovery without sacrificing safety. The need for multicenter randomized studies and standardized protocols remains despite encouraging findings.

Purpose

To examine associations between social isolation and urgency urinary incontinence (UUI) among older women and evaluate anxiety or depression as modifiers.

Method

We conducted a cross-sectional study of women aged ≥65 years in two National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cycles (2015 to 2016 and 2017 to 2018). UUI was defined as leakage in the past year with an urge to urinate. Social isolation was measured using a four-item index and categorized as none, low, or high. Anxiety was defined as feeling worried/nervous at least once per month, and depression as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score ≥5. We used survey-weighted logistic regression.

Results

Among 1,126 older women, 54.1% reported UUI, 42.2% anxiety, and 26.4% depression. Compared to no social isolation, high social isolation was associated with greater odds of UUI (adjusted odds ratio = 1.54, 95% confidence interval [1.02, 2.33], p = .045). Depression (p = .001) was significantly associated with UUI. Depression (pinteraction = .067) and anxiety (pinteraction = .302) were not significant modifiers.

Conclusion

Findings underscore the need for psychosocial screening and integrated support for older women with UUI.

Introduction and hypothesis

Deep endometriosis (DE) may be associated with chronic pelvic pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, psychological distress, and impaired quality of life, though relationships remain poorly characterized. We investigated associations between pelvic floor and lumbopelvic musculoskeletal impairments and psychosocial outcomes in women with DE.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included women aged 18-45 years with DE. Questionnaires assessed quality of life (SF-12), depression (BDI), sexual function (FSFI), kinesiophobia (TSK), and disability (Roland-Morris). Musculoskeletal assessments included vaginal palpation, pain intensity, pressure pain threshold (PPT), flexibility, and functionality. Associations were assessed using Spearman's rho (p < 0.05).

Results

Increased resting pelvic floor muscle tone was observed in 51.1% of participants and myofascial trigger points in 75.6%, more on the left side (71.1%); only 26.7% achieved complete relaxation. PPT was reduced across all muscles, and range of motion was reduced particularly in the hamstrings and iliopsoas. Mean SF-12 scores were 43.92 ± 9.0 (physical) and 54.58 ± 13.61 (mental); 98% had severe depressive symptoms (BDI); mean FSFI score was 24.2 ± 5.6, below the cutoff for sexual dysfunction; kinesiophobia and disability scores were elevated. Objectives

To examine the associations of anticholinergic agents and β3-adrenergic receptor agonists (β3-agonists) prescribed for overactive bladder (OAB) with worsening long-term care needs, incident dementia, and frailty among older women.

Subjects/patients and methods

This retrospective cohort study used the Shizuoka Kokuho Database, a population-based administrative claims database in Japan. Women aged 65-84 years who newly initiated anticholinergic agents or β3-agonists for OAB between 2012 and 2024 and had prescription records consistent with continuous treatment for at least 1 year were included. Follow-up began 12 months after treatment initiation. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (sIPTW) was used to balance baseline covariates between groups. Primary outcomes were worsening long-term care needs and incident dementia; the secondary outcome was changes in the electronic Frailty Index (eFI). Time-to-event outcomes were analyzed using sIPTW-weighted Cox proportional hazards models.

Results

The cohort comprised 1 605 anticholinergic and 2 189 β3-agonist users. After sIPTW, baseline covariates were well-balanced. No significant difference was observed in worsening long-term care needs (hazard ratio [HR], 1.03; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.87-1.22). Anticholinergic use was associated with a higher risk of claims-defined incident dementia compared with β3-agonist use (HR, 1.49; 95% CI, 1.04-2.13). Median eFI did not differ significantly between the groups during 5 years of follow-up.

Conclusion

Among older women with OAB, anticholinergic use was associated with an increased risk of claims-defined incident dementia but not with worsening long-term care needs or frailty compared with β3-agonists. Residual confounding and differential dementia ascertainment cannot be excluded.

Background

Urinary incontinence (UI) is a common geriatric syndrome that adversely affects quality of life. Sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity (SO) may increase vulnerability to UI through the interplay of muscle weakness and excess adiposity, yet their contribution in older women is not well established. This study examined the prevalence of UI across women with sarcopenia and SO and explored its associations with other geriatric syndromes.

Methods

In this cross-sectional study, 535 community-dwelling women aged ≥ 60 years attending a geriatrics outpatient clinic underwent comprehensive geriatric assessment. Sarcopenia risk was screened using the SARC-F questionnaire, muscle strength measured by handgrip dynamometry, and muscle mass estimated via bioelectrical impedance analysis. Obesity was defined by BMI, waist circumference, or body fat percentage, and SO was defined as the coexistence of sarcopenia and obesity. Logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of UI.

Results

UI was reported by 49.9% of participants. Women with UI had higher BMI, more frequent falls, greater frailty, depressive symptoms, higher SARC-F scores, and a greater prevalence of SO. Among the three adjustment methods for SMMI, only BMI-adjusted values showed an association with UI. In multivariable logistic regresion models, fall history (aOR 2.05, 1.38-3.02), SARC-F score (aOR 1.12, 1.02-1.22) and BMI-defined SO (aOR 1.80, 1.09-2.96) independently predicted UI.

Conclusions

SO, sarcopenia risk, and fall history are key determinants of UI in older women. Incorporating muscle and adiposity assessment into continence evaluation may support earlier interventions to maintain continence and independence in this population.

result.abstractText: Urinary retention in older women is a clinically significant and often underdiagnosed condition with complex and multifactorial etiology. Age-related changes in bladder contractile function and bladder sensation, combined with common comorbidities such as neurologic disease, diabetic bladder dysfunction, and pelvic organ prolapse, substantially increase the risk of retention in this population. Medications commonly prescribed to older adults, including anticholinergics and antidepressants, are an often overlooked cause of urinary retention. Evaluation includes a thorough history, physical exam, medication reconciliation, and post-void residual volume, especially because symptoms of retention that are common in men are often non-specific in women. Management should be risk stratified, with acute retention requiring prompt bladder drainage and chronic urinary retention requiring assessment of symptom burden and risk of upper tract deterioration. Pharmacologic treatment options, such as alpha-blockers, have limited evidence in women and broader therapeutic options remain poorly studied in older female populations. Sacral neuromodulation can be effective for non-obstructive urinary retention in older women. This review highlights the critical need for sex-specific and age-specific trials to guide evidence-based patient-centered management of urinary retention in older women.

Objective

This study aimed to evaluate the effects of photobiomodulation (PBM) alone and in combination with pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) on pelvic floor muscle (PFM) function, sexual and urinary function, and quality of life in women with genitourinary syndrome of menopause.

Method

The three-arm clinical trial included women aged 45-65 years who had experienced natural menopause for at least 1 year. Participants were randomized into three groups: PFMT + active PBM, PFMT + sham PBM and isolated PFMT. Interventions lasted 8 weeks, with participants attending two 50-min sessions per week. Outcomes were assessed before and after the 16th session.

Results

Although manometry showed no significant differences between groups, the intervention group demonstrated greater numerical improvement. The Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) total score differed significantly between the PFMT + active PBM and PFMT + sham PBM groups (mean difference = 4.55; 95% confidence interval: 0.57, 8.52; d = 1.05). Significant between-group differences were also observed in the orgasm subdomain in favor of the PFMT + active PBM group compared to the PFMT + sham PBM group. The International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire - short form (ICIQ-SF) indicated a clinically significant improvement of 3.06 points in the PFMT + active PBM group compared to the PFMT + sham PBM group following the intervention.

Conclusion

Active PBM combined with PFMT showed greater but non-significant improvements in PFM pressure, urinary function and quality of life, while significantly improving only sexual function.

Introduction

The hypo-oestrogenic state of the postpartum period leads to bothersome genitourinary symptoms in some lactating women. These symptoms have been named 'Genitourinary Syndrome of Lactation' (GSL), and include vaginal dryness, atrophy, urinary incontinence (UI), urinary tract infection (UTI), delayed wound healing and dyspareunia. Despite its prevalence, the experiences, awareness, quality of life, treatments offered and health-seeking behaviours of mothers with GSL in Australia are unknown.

Methods

A national cross-sectional survey was conducted in Australia, assessing health-seeking behaviours, healthcare provider discussion (provider or patient-initiated), type of healthcare provider, and treatments offered. Quality of life (QoL) was assessed using sliding scales (0-100) to determine the significance of impact across domains.

Results

One hundred and thirteen Australian women, aged 22-48 years responded (mean 33.9). Findings indicated 37% of women were aware of GSL, leaving almost two-thirds unaware. Sixty three percent (n = 65) of women reported at least one genitourinary symptom, with vaginal dryness (57%), urinary incontinence (UI) (27%) and dyspareunia (36%) the most prevalent. Furthermore, one in five respondents reported a healthcare provider-initiated discussion; in contrast, one-third (33%) of respondents reported initiating the discussion. Of respondents, twenty-eight per cent (n = 29) reported being offered treatment, with the primary barrier to treatment (32%) lack of treatment awareness. GSL had a moderate to severe impact on quality of life across the following domains: sexual activity (43%), daily activity (25%), mental health (anxiety, stress, and frustration) (25%) and caring for baby (7%).

Conclusion

A significant proportion of breastfeeding women had GSL symptoms, but many were unaware of the condition. Screening, awareness, and referrals must be enhanced in primary care settings to improve diagnosis, management and minimise barriers to treatment.

Introduction and hypothesis

Urinary incontinence (UI) is common among older women in Jordan and is often not discussed owing to embarrassment and social stigma. Home-based conservative programs may offer a practical and acceptable approach to symptom management. This study was aimed at reaching expert consensus on the essential components of a culturally appropriate, home-based multimodal pelvic health program for Jordanian women aged 55 years and older, using a modified e-Delphi method.

Methods

A two-round modified e-Delphi study was conducted with Jordanian physiotherapists experienced in women's health. In Round 1, experts rated 34 evidence-based items covering pelvic floor muscle training, bladder training, behavioral and lifestyle adjustments, pelvic health education, breathing and postural exercise, adherence support, delivery format, and dosage. Items were rated on a six-point Likert scale, and consensus was defined as ≥ 75% agreement. Items that did not reach consensus were revised and re-rated in Round 2, along with one new subcomponent suggested by the experts.

Results

Nineteen experts completed both rounds. In Round 1, 32 of 34 items reached consensus. In Round 2, the newly proposed subcomponent, whole-body and core strengthening, achieved full consensus. Although weight management did not reach the predefined consensus threshold, it was retained in the final program owing to its clinical importance and evidence-based relevance. Printed educational materials did not achieve consensus and were excluded. The final program consisted of 33 expert-validated components.

Conclusions

This study established expert consensus on the components of a culturally tailored home-based pelvic health program for older Jordanian women with UI. These components provide a practical foundation for program development.

Introduction and hypothesis

Pessary use is a first-line treatment for pelvic organ prolapse (POP). However, complications such as ulcerations, excessive discharge and so on, often compromise treatment adherence, and their risk factors remain poorly characterized. This study is aimed at identifying associated factors for vaginal epithelium-related adverse events (VERAEs) in pessary users.

Methods

This was a secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial, including postmenopausal women with symptomatic POP ≥ stage 2 and successfully fitted with ring pessaries with support. VERAEs were defined as vaginal epithelial abnormalities (erythema, abrasion or erosion/ulceration), vaginal bleeding, or excessive discharge. Participants with and without VERAEs were compared and a multivariable logistic regression model was performed to identify independent factors.

Results

Of 411 women with ≥ 1 follow-up, 119 (29.0%) developed VERAEs. In multivariable regression analysis, longer time since menopause (odds ratio [OR] 1.03, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01-1.07), higher education (undergraduate or higher vs elementary: OR 3.07, 95% CI 1.37-7.03), and advanced prolapse stage (stage 3 vs 2: OR 2.75, 95% CI 1.40-5.74; stage 4 vs 2: OR 3.19, 95% CI 1.20-8.67) were independent risk factors. Protective factors included higher vaginal parity (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52-0.98), active sexual life (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.24-0.76), and continuous estrogen use (≥ 12 months vs none: OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.26-0.77).

Conclusions

Prolonged postmenopausal status, higher education, and severe prolapse increased the risk of VERAEs, whereas increased vaginal parity, active sexual life, and estrogen use are protective factors.

Introduction and hypothesis

Obesity is a recognized risk factor for developing pelvic organ prolapse and for perioperative complications. As the population ages, an increasing number of older, obese individuals with prolapse may opt for surgical repair. This study assesses the association between obesity and short-term perioperative adverse events (AEs) in women ≥ 70 years undergoing vaginal and laparoscopic prolapse surgery.

Methods

This is a secondary analysis of a retrospective cohort study of older women undergoing vaginal and laparoscopic prolapse surgery at two medical centers from 2016 to 2023. Patients were classified as nonobese (< 30 kg/m2), class 1 obese (30-34.9 kg/m2), or class 2+ obese (≥ 35 kg/m2). The primary outcome was composite AEs within 8 weeks after surgery, and secondary outcomes included major AEs and individual AEs.

Results

Of 1507 older women, 20.8% (n = 314) were class 1 obese and 6.0% (n = 90) were class 2+ obese. Obese patients were younger and more likely to be frail, hypertensive, and diabetic (p < 0.05). Obese patients experienced greater estimated intraoperative blood loss (p < 0.05). Obesity was not associated with composite AEs or major AEs on multivariable analysis, but was found to be predictive of postoperative hematoma. Class 1 obese women had a 2.7-times greater odds (95% CI 1.17-6.22) and class 2+ obese women had a 4.7-times greater odds (95% CI 1.61-13.43) of hematoma compared to nonobese women. Obesity was not associated with major hematoma, defined as ≥5 cm or requiring medical or surgical intervention.

Conclusions

Obesity in older surgical patients is not associated with a greater incidence of composite AEs, but may be associated with postoperative hematomas.

Introduction and hypothesis

The objective was to assess the regional variability, mechanical properties, and histological composition of the perineal body in postmenopausal ewes with and without delayed estrogen replacement therapy (ERT), providing data relevant for pelvic floor modeling and the understanding of menopausal tissue changes.

Methods

The fibromuscular layer of the central tendon of the perineal area between the rectum and vagina was used for the study. We analyzed 24 specimens from 8 postmenopausal ewes with ERT (initiated 180 days after ovariectomy and continued for 100 days)-POST-ERT group-and 21 specimens from 7 ewes without ERT-POST group, all 280 days after ovariectomy. Uniaxial tensile tests determined the Young's moduli in small (E0) and large (E1) deformation regions, ultimate stress, and ultimate strain. Histological stereology quantified volume fractions of collagen, elastin, smooth muscle, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue in three regions (R1-R3). Group comparisons and regional analyses were performed using nonparametric statistics.

Results

Mechanical parameters did not differ significantly between groups (E0: 28/25 kPa; E1: 0.38/0.33 MPa; ultimate stress: 0.23/0.23 MPa; ultimate strain: 0.94/0.90 for POST-ERT/POST). ERT was associated with higher collagen (33% versus 23%, p < 0.001) and elastin (6% versus 5%, p < 0.01) content. Regional differences were minimal, with only modest variation in adipose and smooth-muscle fractions and ultimate stress between the midline and lateral regions.

Conclusions

Despite prolonged estrogen deprivation, the perineal body maintained mechanical integrity. Structural changes, particularly increased collagen and elastin after delayed ERT, suggest adaptive remodeling but do not translate into measurable biomechanical reinforcement within the studied timeframe. The results provide parameters for finite element modeling of pelvic floor disorders.

Introduction and hypothesis

Menopause is associated with physiological changes that could alter the muscle mechanical properties (MMPs) of the pelvic floor (PF). This study aimed to investigate the influence of menopause on the mechanical properties of lumbopelvic muscles, with PF muscles as the primary outcome and lumbar paravertebral muscles as a secondary outcome, comparing postmenopausal and premenopausal women while adjusting for age and body mass index (BMI).

Methods

A cross-sectional observational study was conducted involving 20 postmenopausal and 20 premenopausal women aged 45-65 years. MMPs, that is, frequency (tone), stiffness, decrement (inverse of elasticity), and viscoelastic properties (relaxation time of stress, and creep, that represents fluidity), were bilaterally assessed at the PF and lumbar paravertebral level using a device measuring MMPs (MyotonPRO). Sociodemographic and clinical variables (PFDI-20 and PFIQ-7 questionnaires) were also recorded. Between groups comparisons were performed, according to data distribution, and analysis of covariance, adjusted by age and BMI as covariates, were applied to all MMPs of both regions.

Results

Postmenopausal women showed significantly higher values for frequency (1.25 Hz, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.26, 2.23]) and stiffness (40.20 N/m, 95% CI [5.74, 74.66]) on the left side of PF. However, frequency differences were no longer significant after adjustment for age and BMI and left-side stiffness remained associated with age rather than BMI. In contrast, premenopausal women exhibited significantly greater viscoelastic properties at both sides, independently of age and BMI. No significant differences were observed in the MMPs of the lumbar paravertebral muscles (p > 0.05).

Conclusions

MMPs of the PF differed between postmenopausal and premenopausal women. After adjustment for age and BMI, group differences were attenuated; viscoelastic parameters remained different between groups, while increased PF stiffness appeared primarily age-related. No influence by menopausal status was observed at the lumbar level.
